ch02.note: Fourth Avenue (四马路), today Fuzhou Road, was a street of the International Settlement famous for its bookshops, teahouses, theaters and newspaper offices, and notorious for its brothels. The produce market of these opening scenes was a real building at the Fuzhou–Zhejiang Road corner, completed in 1930 and among the most modern in the city; the library on its upper floors, with the disused room behind the stacks, is where the meeting is laid. (Corroborated.)

The Zhejiang Grand Theater (浙江大戏院), on Zhejiang Road directly facing the market, was a real Art Deco cinema of 1930 — the first Shanghai theater by the Hungarian architect László Hudec (邬达克), whose buildings recur through these chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局) governed the foreign-run International Settlement, and its own force, the Municipal Police, policed it. Because the Nationalists' Longhua garrison had no lawful power to make arrests inside the Settlement, it had to work through the Council's police; that jurisdictional seam runs through the whole of the arrest. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: The amusement ground had a forlorn look
ch02.note: The World Hotel (世界大旅社), with its roof-garden amusement ground overlooking the market, is one of the story's Shanghai settings; rooftop pleasure gardens of this kind were a real feature of the Fourth Avenue district, though the sources consulted differ on whether this particular hotel is documented. It is not the famous Great World (大世界) amusement arcade. (Uncorroborated.)

The Lyceum Theatre (兰心大戏院), the Settlement's principal Western theater and home of its British amateur dramatic society, is given here by its standing English name; the building of these years, opened in 1931, still stands on today's Maoming Road South. (Corroborated.)

Cuckoo Soul Abroad (海外鹃魂) was an early 1930s film of the Lianhua company; its star Jin Yan (金焰), a Korea-born actor hailed as the 'Emperor of Film,' played opposite the actress Ziluolan. In classical verse the cuckoo (杜鹃) is said to weep blood for grief, which sharpens Wei Dafu's joke that all three leads end up dead. (Jin Yan and the Lianhua title are corroborated; the film's exact cast is not.)

Longhua (龙华), southwest of the city, was the seat of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison Command and its prison, beside the Longhua Temple and its ancient pagoda. In February 1931 the Nationalists secretly shot some two dozen Communists here—the 'Longhua Martyrs,' among them the 'Five Martyrs' of the League of Left-Wing Writers (Rou Shi, Hu Yepin, Yin Fu, Feng Keng and Li Weisen), a killing mourned by Lu Xun. It is to this garrison that the prisoners of the novel are taken. (Corroborated.)

The Generalissimo (委员长) is Chiang Kai-shek (蒋介石, 1887–1975), chairman of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission and head of the KMT government and army. In the winter of 1932–33, the novel's moment, he was directing the Fourth Encirclement Campaign against the Communists' Central Soviet. (Corroborated.)

Mount Lu (庐山, Lushan), above Jiujiang in Jiangxi, was the Nationalist government's summer seat, where Chiang Kai-shek kept a villa and transacted business of state; a petitioner such as Du Yuesheng seeking the Generalissimo's ear would indeed go up the mountain. (Corroborated.)

The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (招商局), founded by the Qing statesman Li Hongzhang (here 'Grand Secretary Li'), was at the center of a real 1933 scandal. Li's grandson Li Guojie (李国杰), who ran one of its arms, was accused of mortgaging the company's Shanghai wharves—among them the Jinliyuan of the earlier scene—for a vast loan and pocketing the kickback, with Chen Fumu (陈孚木) as a go-between; a Shanghai court sentenced Li to eight years in April 1933. The gangster Du Yuesheng (the 'tycoon Du') hovers behind the affair as the detectives gossip it. (Corroborated; Du's exact role is not settled by the sources.)

ch03.note: The Central Party Affairs Investigation Section (党务调查科) was the Kuomintang's political-intelligence organ, run under the Central Organization Department by the Chen brothers' 'CC Clique' and from 1929 by Xu Enzeng; those in the know called its Nanjing base, in the Zhanyuan garden, the 'Special Operations Headquarters.' It was the forerunner of the wartime Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (中统). You Tianxiao's secret post in it, outranking his open one, is the source of his double-dealing. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the 32nd Army of the National Revolutionary Army
ch03.note: A 32nd Army of the National Revolutionary Army did exist, but it was Shang Zhen's (商震) Shanxi–Suiyuan force, stationed in Hebei in 1931–33, not at Shanghai; the units that actually held Longhua under the Songhu Garrison Command were others. Posting a '32nd Army' to the Shanghai garrison is the novel's own detail, not the historical record. (Contradicted.)

The pagoda beside the garrison is the ancient Longhua Pagoda, standardly 龙华塔; Bao'en Pagoda (报恩塔, 'Pagoda of Requited Kindness') is a genuine traditional alternate name for it, from the legend that Sun Quan of Wu raised it to repay his mother. The source thus uses a historically valid variant, not a mistake. (Corroborated.)

Xi Shi (西施), a legendary beauty of the state of Yue in the Spring and Autumn era, was by tradition sent to beguile the king of rival Wu and hasten its ruin—the archetypal planted agent. As a cryptonym for a mole inside the enemy's ranks it is pointed; the identity of 'Xi Shi' is one of the book's central secrets.

ch04.anchor: Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic
ch04.note: The Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic (危害民国紧急治罪法), promulgated by the Nationalist government on 31 January 1931, prescribed death for a range of acts against the state and was the chief legal instrument used against Communists; hence the interrogator's threat of the firing squad. (Corroborated.)

Haohan (浩瀚, 'the vast') is the working alias of a senior Communist the enemy is hunting; within the Party he was known for articles published under the name in The Guide Weekly (向导), the Central Committee's organ of the 1920s. His whereabouts, and who among the arrested may be his contact, are the engine of the plot.

Winter (冬) is Ling Wen's own novel, a book within the book; like Ling Wen and the other principals it is the author's invention. The novel's protagonists are fictional, set against a real historical background; its closing appendix frames the whole as an homage to the real, largely nameless Communists executed at Longhua. (The title Winter echoes the name of Ling Wen's late husband, Long Dong, 龙冬.)

The May Thirtieth Movement (五卅运动) was the wave of anti-imperialist strikes and protests that swept China after Settlement police shot Chinese demonstrators in Shanghai on 30 May 1925; it drew many, like Ling Wen and her husband, into the revolution. The Northern Expedition she goes on to mention set out from Guangzhou in 1926; the Nationalist purge of Communists began in 1927. (Corroborated.)

Tanhuang (滩簧) opera is a family of Jiangnan folk sung-drama forms in the Wu dialect, out of which grew Shanghai opera (沪剧) and its Suzhou and Wuxi cousins; the comparison casts Miss Tao's laughter as broad and theatrical. (Corroborated.)

ch05.note: Da Hong Pao (大红袍, 'Great Red Robe') is the most storied of the Wuyi 'rock teas,' a heavily oxidized oolong grown on the cliffs of Mount Wuyi in Fujian and long counted among the most prized teas in China.

The Nineteenth Route Army (十九路军) was the Cantonese force that put up fierce resistance to the Japanese at Shanghai in the 'January 28' Incident of 1932 (一·二八, the first Battle of Shanghai); it was afterwards sent to fight Communists in Fujian. 'Commander Cai' is the army's general Cai Tingkai (蔡廷锴). (Corroborated.)

Xuanwu Lake (玄武湖) lies against the northeastern wall of Nanjing; the drive in this chapter runs beside its stretch of the great Ming-dynasty city wall, past Jiming Temple (鸡鸣寺) and out by the Shence Gate (神策门). Nanjing was the Nationalist capital and the seat of the secret-service headquarters to which You Tianxiao reports.

ch06.note: The encirclement and suppression campaigns (围剿) were the Nationalists' successive military drives from 1930 against the Communist base areas, above all the Central Soviet (中央苏区) in Jiangxi–Fujian, whose capital was Ruijin; the Communists fought them as 'counter-encirclement.' The Fourth was under way in the winter of 1932–33. In the movement's usual geography the country divided into 'Red' or Soviet areas and the 'White areas' (白区) under Nationalist rule, where the novel's underground works. (Corroborated.)

Brigade Commander Weng is Weng Zhaoyuan (翁照垣, 1892–1972), a brigade commander of the Nineteenth Route Army who took the first Japanese assault at Zhabei on the night of 28 January 1932; both the man and the Zhabei defense are historical. He is a different man from the Cantonese 'Adjutant Weng' of the earlier chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Guangzhou Uprising (广州起义, the Canton Uprising of 11–13 December 1927) was a Communist insurrection that briefly proclaimed a 'Guangzhou Commune' before being crushed with heavy loss of life — the last of the failed urban risings of 1927. (Corroborated.)

ch06.anchor: There are no miracles in nature or history
ch06.note: The lines Chen Qianyuan is translating are the opening of Lenin's Letters from Afar (远方来信), First Letter, written from Zurich in March 1917; the wording here follows the standard English of Lenin's Collected Works. The next chapter of the novel takes its title, 'A Letter from Afar,' from this same work. (Corroborated.)

ch07.note: In early 1933 Chiang Kai-shek directed the anti-Communist campaigns in person from Nanchang (南昌), Jiangxi; his formal Nanchang Field Headquarters (南昌行营) followed in May 1933, the forward command post for the Fourth and Fifth Encirclement Campaigns. (Corroborated.)

Xinjing (新京, 'New Capital,' today Changchun) was the capital of Manchukuo (满洲国), the puppet state Japan proclaimed in the occupied Northeast in March 1932. A merchant 'from Xinjing' in 1933 Shanghai is thus a man arriving from Japanese-held Manchuria — a loaded provenance, and part of Chen Qianli's cover. (Corroborated.)

Shanhaiguan (山海关), the pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, was stormed and taken by Japanese forces on 1–3 January 1933, opening the Defense of the Great Wall campaign (长城抗战) as Japan pushed south from Manchuria; it fixes the novel's atmosphere of national crisis. (Corroborated.)
Shen Bao (申报), founded in 1872 and published in Shanghai, was the most important Chinese-language newspaper of the Republican era. (Corroborated.)

Khabarovsk (伯力), in the Soviet Far East, places Chen Qianli's three years of training in the USSR — the Soviet and Comintern schooling that stood behind many senior Chinese Communist operatives of the period; his long way out (Khabarovsk to Vladivostok, then by sea) follows a real clandestine route. The school itself is the novel's; the geography is real.

The Outpost (前哨) was the organ of the League of Left-Wing Writers; its first issue (April 1931), edited by Lu Xun (鲁迅) and Feng Xuefeng (冯雪峰), was a memorial number for the writers murdered at Longhua weeks before. This stretch of North Sichuan Road (北四川路) in Hongkou was the heart of the leftist literary world; Chen Geng (陈赓), the Red Army commander named here, really did meet Lu Xun secretly in Shanghai in 1932. (Corroborated.)

The Yihong Garden (扆虹园), a Cantonese garden-mansion in the North Sichuan Road quarter, was visited more than once by Sun Yat-sen (孙中山, 'Mr. Sun') — in 1912–13 Guangdong native-place associations fêted him there. (Corroborated.)

The Left League is the League of Left-Wing Writers (左联), founded in Shanghai in 1930; five of its young members were among the Communists shot at Longhua in February 1931 whom the novel commemorates. (Corroborated.)
The Nanchang Uprising (南昌起义) of 1 August 1927 was the Communists' first armed revolt against the Nationalists, afterwards marked as the founding day of the Red Army. (Corroborated.)

The German Hospital (德国医院) was the real Paulun Hospital (宝隆医院), founded in 1900 by the German physician Erich Paulun and tied to what became Tongji University's medical school; it stood in the Settlement, and its later descendant is Shanghai's Changzheng Hospital. (Corroborated.)

ch08.note: The Grand Theatre (大光明大戏院), on today's West Nanjing Road, was Shanghai's most celebrated cinema; the László Hudec rebuild that made it an Art Deco landmark was completed in mid-1933, just as this chapter is set. (Corroborated.)

Marlene Dietrich (玛琳·黛德丽, 1901–1992), the German-American film star, had lately played 'Shanghai Lily' in Shanghai Express (1932); her face on a Shanghai cinema hoarding in 1933 is exactly of its moment. (Corroborated.)

Turandot, Puccini's last opera (premiered posthumously in 1926), is set in a legendary Peking whose princess beheads the suitors who fail her riddles; the poster's line condenses the opera's blood-soaked opening — the executioner's chorus, 'Gira la cote' ('turn the grindstone') — rather than quoting it. The touring San Carlo company was real, though a 1933 Carlton staging is not separately documented. (The opera corroborated; the Shanghai performance uncorroborated.)

As the Japanese advanced in early 1933, the Palace Museum in Beiping (北平, as Beijing was then called) began evacuating its treasures south; the first crates left the Forbidden City on the night of 5–6 February 1933, and the removal filled the newspapers exactly as the chapter describes. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: the Four Banks' Savings Society building
ch08.note: The tower going up across from the racecourse is the Park Hotel (国际饭店), developed by the Joint Savings Society of four banks (四行储蓄会) to a design by László Hudec and completed in 1934; at twenty-two storeys it was the tallest building in Asia for nearly thirty years. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: the Four Masters of the Ming
ch08.note: The Four Masters of the Ming (明四家) are Shen Zhou, Wen Zhengming, Tang Yin and Qiu Ying (仇英); Qiu Ying alone was a professional artisan-painter, a master of meticulous brushwork whose much-prized manner made him one of the most heavily forged names in Chinese painting — apt for a tale of a fake. (Corroborated.)
The racecourse is the great oval of the Shanghai Race Club, a center of foreign social life; its grounds are today People's Square and People's Park. (Corroborated.)
The Grand Champagne (大香槟) was the Race Club's celebrated sweepstakes lottery, drawn on the big races; here the split ticket serves the plot as a recognition token. (Corroborated.)
The Xiaolin Guangji (笑林广记, 'Expanded Forest of Laughter') is the best-known of the classical Chinese joke-books, compiled in the Qing dynasty. (Corroborated.)

Morriss (马立斯) renders the name of the British Morriss family, proprietors of the North-China Daily News; the transliteration is well attested in old Shanghai, though the particular building named here, by the racecourse, is not separately documented. (The name corroborated; the building uncorroborated.)
